# From tissue chemistry to clinical interpretation

My research focuses on **how chemical elements, particles and molecular processes can be mapped, quantified and interpreted in human disease**. The programme combines elemental imaging, cancer sciences, environmental and occupational health and clinical biochemistry.
</div>

## Research themes

:::: {.grid .research-grid}
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
<div class="card-label">01</div>

### Elemental pathology

Development of tissue elemental imaging workflows using **laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS)**, with the aim of locating and quantifying metals and particle-associated elemental signatures directly in biological specimens.

Key questions include analytical validation, spatial heterogeneity, tissue preparation, semi-quantification and clinical interpretability.

[BioLIBS platform →](biolibs.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
<div class="card-label">02</div>

### Environmental & occupational exposure

Mapping exogenous elements and mineral particles in lung tissue to better understand past exposure and its possible relationship with chronic respiratory disease.

Applications include interstitial lung disease, sarcoidosis, emphysema and occupational lung disease.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
<div class="card-label">03</div>

### Cancer sciences & nanomedicine

Translational research in tumor biology, molecular imaging, nanomedicine and theranostics, including strategies designed to improve tumor detection, biodistribution assessment and therapeutic targeting.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .research-card}
<div class="card-label">04</div>

### Clinical translation

Development of clinically robust workflows from archived tissue studies to prospective and multicentre studies, with attention to reproducibility, pathology correlation, method validation and future diagnostic implementation.

[Clinical research →](clinical-research.qmd)
:::
::::

## Methods and technology

My group combines **LIBS elemental imaging** with complementary approaches such as electron microscopy/EDX, Raman or FTIR spectroscopy, synchrotron micro-XRF and mass-spectrometry-based elemental analysis when scientifically appropriate.

The emphasis is not on one instrument alone, but on choosing the combination of methods that best answers the biological or clinical question.

## Translational philosophy

<div class="quote-panel">
**What is present in a tissue? Where is it located? What does it mean for disease, exposure or patient care?**

These three questions structure much of my research. The objective is to connect analytical chemistry with pathology and medicine, rather than generating elemental maps in isolation.
</div>
